title: The first people arrive in Japan
text:
Japan is a country made of islands: four big ones (Hokkaido, Honshu, Shikoku and Kyushu) and more than 14,000 small ones! But a very long time ago, things looked different.

About 40,000 years ago, the Earth was in an [Ice Age]. So much water was frozen into ice that the sea level was more than 100 metres lower than today. In some places, you could almost walk from the Asian continent to the islands of Japan, and the sea straits were much narrower.

The first humans arrived in Japan around this time, probably around 38,000 years ago. They came from the continent, following animals they hunted. Some may have come by land in the north, others crossed the sea in small boats. Imagine the courage it took to paddle toward an island you could barely see!

These first inhabitants were [hunter-gatherers]. They did not grow crops or keep animals. They moved from place to place, hunting big animals like [Naumann's elephant] (a kind of elephant with long tusks), giant deer and wild boar. They also gathered nuts, berries and roots, and caught fish.

They made tools out of stone. Archaeologists have found thousands of sharp stone blades, axes and scrapers. Some of the oldest polished stone axes in the whole world have been found in Japan! Stone from volcanoes, called [obsidian], was especially good for making razor-sharp knives. Interestingly, obsidian from the small island of Kozushima was found on the main island, which proves people were already travelling by sea.

They lived in simple shelters made of branches and animal skins, or in caves. They gathered around fires to stay warm during the long, cold winters.

This very long period, before people made pottery, is called the [Paleolithic] or Old Stone Age.

About 15,000 years ago, the Ice Age ended. The ice melted, the sea rose, and Japan became the group of islands we know today. Forests grew, and the big animals slowly disappeared. People had to change their way of life... and that is when something new was invented: pottery!

title: Jōmon: some of the oldest pottery in the world
text:
After the Ice Age, Japan became warmer and covered in forests full of chestnut trees, acorns, deer and wild boar. The seas were full of fish and shellfish. Life became a bit easier.

Around 16,000 to 14,000 years ago, the people of Japan invented something amazing: pottery. They shaped clay into pots and baked them in fire. Some of these pots are among the oldest in the whole world!

Why was this so important? With a pot, you can boil food! People could now cook soups and stews, soften hard acorns and chestnuts, and cook shellfish. They could also store food for the winter.

These people decorated their pots by pressing twisted cords into the wet clay, which made patterns like rope. In Japanese, "rope pattern" is "Jōmon". That's why this long period of history, which lasted more than 10,000 years, is called the Jōmon period!

Some Jōmon pots are incredible works of art. The "flame-style" pots from Niigata look like they are covered in dancing flames or waves.

The Jōmon people were still [hunter-gatherers], but many of them stopped moving around. They built villages of [pit dwellings]: round houses dug a little into the ground, with a roof of wood and thatch, a bit like a big tent. A fireplace in the middle kept everyone warm.

They left behind huge piles of shells called [shell mounds]. For archaeologists, these are treasure troves! In them, they find fish bones, broken tools, jewellery... it's like looking into the Jōmon people's rubbish bins.

The Jōmon people also made mysterious clay figures called [dogū]. Some have huge eyes that look like snow goggles! Nobody knows exactly what they were for. Maybe they were used in ceremonies, to pray for health, for babies to be born safely, or for good hunting.

They also made jewellery from jade, shells and animal teeth, and lacquered red objects.

The Jōmon period shows that people can build a rich culture that lasts thousands of years, even without farming.

title: Sannai-Maruyama, a big Jōmon village
text:
In 1992, workers in Aomori, in the far north of Honshu, were getting ready to build a baseball stadium. When they started digging, they found something that surprised everyone: the remains of a huge Jōmon village! The stadium was never built. Instead, the site became one of the most famous archaeological sites in Japan: Sannai-Maruyama.

People lived there for about 1,500 years, from around 3900 to 2200 BC. At certain times, several hundred people may have lived there together. That's a big village for the time!

Archaeologists found the remains of more than 700 [pit dwellings], where families lived. They also found a very long building, 32 metres long, which may have been a meeting hall or a workshop for the whole village.

The most impressive discovery was six enormous holes, each with the remains of a giant chestnut tree trunk, about one metre wide! Together they held up a huge wooden tower, maybe 15 metres high. What was it for? A watchtower? A temple? A lighthouse for people fishing at sea? Nobody knows for sure. Today, a reconstruction of this tower stands on the site.

The villagers ate chestnuts, walnuts, fish, rabbits and flying squirrels. They even seem to have planted and cared for chestnut trees near the village. This shows they were starting to manage nature, even though they did not grow rice yet.

They traded with faraway places. Archaeologists found [jade] that came from Niigata, hundreds of kilometres away, and [obsidian] from Hokkaido. They also found [lacquer] objects, painted a beautiful red, and small woven baskets.

The villagers buried their dead in rows of graves along a road. Babies were buried in pots near the houses, perhaps so that they would stay close to their families.

In 2021, Sannai-Maruyama and other Jōmon sites in Hokkaido and northern Japan were listed as a [UNESCO World Heritage] site. Today, you can visit the site, see reconstructed houses, and even try making Jōmon pottery yourself!

title: Yayoi: rice fields and bronze bells
text:
Rice is the heart of Japanese cuisine. But it has not always been grown in Japan! Rice farming came from the Asian continent, through Korea, and began in northern Kyushu around 1000 to 300 BC. It then spread slowly across Japan.

This new period is called the Yayoi period, after a neighbourhood in Tokyo where a new kind of pottery was first found in 1884.

Growing rice in [paddy fields] changed everything. A paddy field is a flat field flooded with water. Building one is hard work: people had to level the ground, dig channels to bring water from rivers, and build little walls to keep the water in. They needed to work together, as a big team. So people began to live in larger villages, with leaders to organize the work.

Rice could be stored for a long time. People built [raised storehouses] on stilts, so that mice and damp could not reach the rice. Families who had more rice became richer and more powerful than others. For the first time in Japan, there were rich and poor people, chiefs and workers.

New people also came from the continent, bringing new skills, especially working with metal. The Yayoi people used iron for tools and weapons, and [bronze] for beautiful objects: mirrors, swords, and mysterious bells called [dōtaku]. These bells were probably used in ceremonies to pray for a good harvest. Some have little drawings of people pounding rice, deer, and dragonflies!

Unfortunately, where there are riches, there are also fights. Some Yayoi villages were surrounded by deep ditches and wooden fences to protect them from attacks. The most famous is [Yoshinogari] in Saga prefecture, with watchtowers and houses you can visit today.

Chinese history books from this time talk about Japan for the first time. They call it the "Land of Wa" and say it was divided into more than 100 small countries.

The Yayoi period lasted until about AD 250. Its rice fields are still the landscape of Japan today!

title: Queen Himiko of Yamatai
text:
The first person from Japan whose name we know was... a queen! Her name was Himiko.

We don't know about her from Japanese books, because the Japanese did not write yet. We know about her thanks to a Chinese history book called the "Records of Wei", written around the year 280.

According to this book, the Land of Wa (Japan) had been at war for many years. The small countries fought each other. Finally, they agreed to choose a woman as their ruler: Himiko, queen of a country called Yamatai.

Himiko was a kind of [shaman]. People believed she could talk with the spirits and gods. She lived in a palace guarded by soldiers, and very few people ever saw her. The book says she had 1,000 women servants, but only one man was allowed to bring her food and carry her messages. Her younger brother helped her govern.

In the year 239, Himiko sent ambassadors across the sea to the powerful Chinese kingdom of Wei. She sent gifts, including cloth and people. The Chinese emperor was pleased. He gave her the title "Queen of Wa, Friend of Wei", a golden seal, and 100 bronze mirrors!

When Himiko died, around 248, a big [burial mound] was built for her. After her death, a king took her place, but the fighting started again. Peace only returned when a 13-year-old girl called Iyo, a relative of Himiko, became queen.

Where was Yamatai? It's one of the biggest mysteries in Japanese history! Some historians think it was in northern Kyushu. Others think it was in the Nara region, where the Japanese state would later be born. Scholars have been arguing about it for over 300 years! Some think a big old tomb in Nara, called Hashihaka, might be Himiko's.

Whatever the answer, Himiko shows that in early Japan, women could hold great power and religious authority. She is still a popular character today, appearing in manga, video games and even as the name of a boat in Tokyo!

title: The giant keyhole tombs
text:
If you look at the city of Sakai, near Osaka, from an airplane, you can see something strange: a huge green shape in the middle of the houses, shaped like an old-fashioned keyhole, surrounded by water. What is it? It's a giant tomb!

From about 250 to 600, powerful chiefs in Japan were buried in enormous earth mounds called kofun. That's why this period is called the Kofun period.

The biggest one is the Daisen Kofun, traditionally said to be the tomb of Emperor Nintoku. It is 486 metres long, longer than five football fields! It's one of the largest tombs in the world, bigger in area than the Great Pyramid of Egypt. Historians think it took about 2,000 workers more than 15 years to build it, moving the earth by hand with baskets.

Why a keyhole shape? Nobody knows for sure. The round part was where the body was buried. The square part may have been used for ceremonies.

The slopes of the mounds were decorated with thousands of clay figures called [haniwa]. There were simple tubes, but also houses, horses, boats, warriors in armour, dancers, and even dogs and chickens. They were like guardians protecting the dead chief. Some haniwa have such funny faces that they look like cartoon characters!

Inside the tombs, archaeologists found treasures: bronze mirrors, iron swords, armour, horse gear, and jewellery made of curved beads called [magatama].

These giant tombs show that during this time, a powerful group of chiefs in the Nara and Osaka region became stronger and stronger. This group was called the [Yamato] court. Its leader was the "great king", who later became known as the [Emperor]. Little by little, the Yamato kings brought much of Japan under their control.

Many people came from Korea during this time, bringing new skills: making hard grey pottery, weaving silk, working metal, and writing with Chinese characters.

In 2019, 49 kofun around Sakai were listed as a UNESCO World Heritage site. Most of them are still considered sacred, and nobody is allowed to dig inside!

title: Buddhism arrives in Japan
text:
Before the 6th century, the people of Japan followed their own traditional religion, later called [Shinto], "the way of the gods". They believed that countless gods and spirits, called [kami], lived in nature: in mountains, trees, rocks, rivers, the sun and the wind. They honoured them at shrines with offerings and festivals.

In 538 (or 552, according to other sources), a king from Korea, of the kingdom of Baekje, sent the Japanese court a gift: a golden statue of the Buddha and some Buddhist books.

[Buddhism] was a religion born in India about 1,000 years earlier. It teaches that life is full of suffering, but that people can be freed from it by living wisely and kindly, and by meditating, following the example of the [Buddha], "the awakened one".

The Japanese court did not know what to do with this gift. Some powerful families were against it. The Mononobe clan said: "If we worship a foreign god, our own kami will be angry!" But the [Soga clan] liked the new religion and wanted to adopt it.

The legend says that when the Soga built a temple for the statue, a terrible disease spread. The Mononobe said it was the anger of the kami, and they threw the Buddha statue into a canal! But the disease did not stop...

The two families argued for about 50 years, and finally fought a war. In 587, the Soga won. From then on, Buddhism was supported by the court.

Buddhism brought many new things to Japan: temples with curved roofs, statues, paintings, new ideas, and a lot of knowledge from China and Korea, like architecture, medicine and writing.

What's special in Japan is that Buddhism did not replace Shinto. The two religions learned to live together, and even mixed. Many Japanese people today visit a Shinto shrine for New Year and for a baby's birth, get married in a Christian-style or Shinto ceremony, and have a Buddhist funeral. People say: "born Shinto, die Buddhist"!

title: Prince Shōtoku and the 17-article constitution
text:
Prince Shōtoku is one of the most famous people in Japanese history. For a long time, his face was even printed on Japanese banknotes!

He lived from 574 to 622, during the [Asuka period], named after the area near Nara where the court was. He was the nephew of Empress Suiko, the first woman to be empress of Japan, and he helped her govern as her [regent].

Many legends are told about him. It is said that he was born in front of a stable, and that he was so clever he could listen to ten people speaking at the same time and answer each one correctly! That's why he is sometimes shown with a special name meaning "prince with ten ears".

Shōtoku wanted to make Japan a strong, well-organized country, like China, which was then the most advanced country in Asia. In 604, he wrote the Seventeen-Article Constitution. It was not a constitution like today's, but a list of rules for government officials. The very first article says: "Harmony is to be valued." Other articles say officials should work hard, be honest, not be greedy, and respect Buddhism.

He also created a system of 12 ranks for officials, shown by the colour of their caps. People could be promoted for their talent, not only because of their family.

In 607, Shōtoku sent an ambassador, Ono no Imoko, to China. His letter to the Chinese emperor began: "From the Son of Heaven in the land where the sun rises, to the Son of Heaven in the land where the sun sets." The Chinese emperor was not happy that Japan dared to call itself equal! But this is one of the first times Japan was described as the land of the rising sun.

Shōtoku was a devoted Buddhist. He built many temples, including Hōryū-ji near Nara. Its buildings, rebuilt shortly after a fire in 670, are the oldest wooden buildings in the world! You can still visit them today.

Today, some historians think that many of the stories about Shōtoku were exaggerated after his death, but he remains a symbol of wisdom and harmony.

title: Nara, the first great capital, and the oldest books
text:
Before 710, the Japanese capital moved each time a new emperor came to the throne. That was not very practical! So the government decided to build a big, permanent capital, following the model of Chang'an, the capital of China, the largest city in the world at the time.

In 710, the new capital Heijō-kyō was completed in what is today the city of Nara. It was laid out like a giant chessboard, with straight streets crossing at right angles. The main avenue, Suzaku Avenue, was 74 metres wide! At the north end stood the imperial palace. Maybe 100,000 people lived in the city.

This period, from 710 to 794, is called the Nara period.

The government was organized according to new laws inspired by China, called the [Ritsuryō] system. All the land belonged to the emperor, and farmers received rice fields and had to pay taxes in rice, cloth or work.

During this time, the Japanese wrote their first history books. In 712, the Kojiki ("Record of Ancient Matters") was finished. It tells the myths of Japan's creation: how the gods Izanagi and Izanami stirred the ocean with a spear and created the islands; how the sun goddess [Amaterasu] hid in a cave and plunged the world into darkness, until the other gods made her come out by throwing a noisy party! The Kojiki says the emperors are descended from Amaterasu.

In 720, a longer history book, the Nihon Shoki, was completed.

Around 759, a huge collection of about 4,500 poems was put together: the Man'yōshū. It contains poems by emperors and nobles, but also by soldiers, farmers and fishermen. Japanese people still love these poems today. In fact, the name of today's era, "Reiwa", comes from a poem in the Man'yōshū!

At that time, Japanese was written using Chinese characters, which was very complicated. Sometimes the characters were used for their meaning, sometimes just for their sound.

Today in Nara, you can still see the remains of the palace, and over a thousand friendly deer walk freely in the parks. They even bow to get special crackers!

title: The Great Buddha of Tōdai-ji
text:
In the 730s, Japan was going through hard times. There were earthquakes, droughts, famine, rebellions, and a terrible [smallpox] epidemic that killed about a third of the population, including important ministers.

The emperor at the time, Emperor Shōmu, was a devoted Buddhist. He believed that the Buddha could protect the country. So in 743, he announced a gigantic project: to build a huge bronze statue of the Buddha in the capital, Nara, and a temple big enough to hold it.

This project needed enormous resources. It is said that more than 2.6 million people helped in some way, by giving money, materials or work. A famous monk named Gyōki, who was loved by ordinary people because he built bridges, roads and ponds for them, travelled the country to gather support.

Making the statue was an enormous technical challenge. The workers built a clay model, then poured melted bronze over it in eight layers, from the bottom to the top. They used about 500 tonnes of copper! Then the statue was covered in gold.

In 752, a great ceremony took place to "open the eyes" of the Buddha. An Indian monk painted the eyes with a giant brush. Monks and musicians came from China, Korea and even further away. It was one of the biggest international events of the time!

The statue shows the [Vairocana] Buddha, the cosmic Buddha who shines on the whole universe. It is about 15 metres high. Its hand alone is taller than an adult! The temple that houses it, the Great Buddha Hall of Tōdai-ji, is one of the largest wooden buildings in the world.

The statue and the hall have been damaged by fires and earthquakes several times, and rebuilt. The current hall dates from 1709 and is a bit smaller than the original!

Here's a fun tradition: in one of the wooden pillars of the hall, there is a hole the same size as one of the Buddha's nostrils. People say that if you can crawl through it, you will be wise and happy. Children often try it!

Next to Tōdai-ji is the Shōsōin, a wooden storehouse that still contains treasures from Emperor Shōmu, including objects that came along the Silk Road from Persia!

title: Heian-kyō: Kyoto becomes the capital
text:
At the end of the Nara period, Buddhist temples in Nara had become very rich and powerful. Some monks even tried to take part in politics! The Emperor Kanmu wanted to get away from their influence. So he decided to move the capital.

In 794, the new capital was founded: Heian-kyō, which means "capital of peace and tranquillity". Today, we know it as [Kyoto].

Like Nara, it was laid out like a giant grid, following the Chinese model. It was surrounded by mountains on three sides, which was considered lucky and protective according to the Chinese art of placement, called [feng shui]. Two rivers flowed nearby. The main avenue was more than 80 metres wide!

Kyoto remained the capital of Japan, where the emperor lived, for more than 1,000 years, until 1868! That's why Kyoto is full of old temples, shrines and palaces. Today, it has 17 UNESCO World Heritage sites.

The period from 794 to 1185 is called the Heian period. For almost 400 years, there were very few wars in Japan. It was a golden age for art and culture at the imperial court.

Little by little, the emperors lost their real power. A noble family, the [Fujiwara clan], became the true rulers. How did they do it? By marrying their daughters to the emperors! The emperor's grandfather or father-in-law was then a Fujiwara, who governed in the name of the young emperor, as [regent]. The most famous of them, Fujiwara no Michinaga, was so powerful that he wrote a poem saying he was like the full moon, perfect and complete!

In 1053, Michinaga's son built the Byōdō-in, a beautiful temple with a hall shaped like a phoenix spreading its wings, reflected in a pond. It was supposed to look like the Buddhist paradise. You can see it on the 10-yen coin!

Meanwhile, far from the capital, in the provinces, a new kind of person was appearing: warriors on horseback, skilled with the bow, who protected the lands of the nobles. They would soon become very important: the [samurai].

title: Kana and The Tale of Genji
text:
Japanese children learn three kinds of writing: [kanji], [hiragana] and [katakana]. Do you know where hiragana and katakana come from? From the Heian period!

For a long time, the Japanese wrote only with Chinese characters, kanji. But Chinese and Japanese are very different languages. So around the 9th century, people began to simplify some Chinese characters to write the sounds of Japanese. That's how the [kana] were born.

Katakana were made from parts of Chinese characters, and were first used by monks to take notes when reading Buddhist texts. Hiragana were made from Chinese characters written in a flowing, rounded style. They were easy to write and pretty to look at.

At the imperial court, men were expected to write in Chinese, like serious scholars. Hiragana were often called "women's hand", because women at the court used them a lot. And the women of the Heian court used them to write some of the greatest works of Japanese literature!

The most famous is The Tale of Genji, written around the year 1000 by a lady-in-waiting known as Murasaki Shikibu. It tells the story of Prince Genji, handsome and talented, his loves, his friendships, his sorrows, and the life of his children. It has 54 chapters and more than 400 characters! Many people consider it the first [novel] in the world. It is still read today, and has been made into manga, films and plays.

At the same time, another lady, Sei Shōnagon, wrote "The Pillow Book". It's a kind of diary full of lists, observations and funny opinions. It begins: "In spring, it is the dawn..." She wrote lists like "Things that make the heart beat faster" and "Hateful things", such as a guest who talks on and on when you're in a hurry!

Heian nobles loved poetry. They wrote short poems of 31 syllables called [waka] to express their feelings, and exchanged them in letters. Choosing the right paper, the perfect handwriting and a nice perfume was very important!

The famous poem to learn hiragana, "Iroha", which uses each kana exactly once, also dates from this time.

title: The Genpei War: Taira against Minamoto
text:
By the 12th century, [samurai] warriors had become powerful. Two great samurai families were rivals: the Taira clan (also called Heike), whose colour was red, and the Minamoto clan (also called Genji), whose colour was white.

At first, the Taira won. Their leader, Taira no Kiyomori, became the most powerful man in Japan. He even married his daughter to the emperor, and his grandson became emperor as a baby. Kiyomori spared the lives of some young Minamoto boys... a big mistake for him!

In 1180, the Minamoto rose up. This started a great civil war called the Genpei War, from the Chinese readings of the two family names: "Gen" for Minamoto and "Hei" for Taira.

The most famous hero of this war was a young Minamoto general: Minamoto no Yoshitsune. According to legend, as a child he learned swordsmanship from mountain goblins called tengu! He was a brilliant general. In one famous attack, he led his horsemen down a cliff so steep that the Taira thought nobody could come from there.

His loyal companion was a giant warrior-monk named Benkei. The legend says that Benkei had defeated 999 warriors on a bridge in Kyoto and taken their swords, but lost the 1,000th fight against young Yoshitsune, and became his faithful follower.

The final battle took place at sea, at Dan-no-ura, in 1185, between Honshu and Kyushu. At first, the tide helped the Taira. But then it turned, and the Minamoto won. Rather than be captured, many Taira jumped into the sea. The grandmother of the child Emperor Antoku, only 6 years old, took him in her arms and jumped into the waves with him. It's one of the saddest stories in Japanese history.

The story of this war is told in "The Tale of the Heike". Blind monks travelled around Japan singing it while playing the [biwa], a kind of lute. It begins: "The sound of the bells of the Gion temple echoes the impermanence of all things..." meaning that power never lasts forever.

A legend says that the crabs of this sea have faces like angry samurai on their shells: the spirits of the Taira warriors!

title: The first shogun: the Kamakura shogunate
text:
After winning the Genpei War, the leader of the Minamoto clan, Minamoto no Yoritomo, became the most powerful man in Japan. But he did not try to become emperor. Instead, he did something new.

He set up his own government far from Kyoto, in the town of Kamakura, near today's Tokyo. In 1192, the emperor gave him the title of [shogun], which means "great general who subdues the barbarians". This military government was called the [shogunate] or bakufu, which means "tent government", because a general directs his army from a tent!

From then on, for almost 700 years, Japan had two centres of power: the emperor in Kyoto, who was respected and performed ceremonies but had little real power, and the shogun, who controlled the army and really governed the country.

This was the beginning of the age of the [samurai]. The samurai were professional warriors who served a lord. The shogun gave his loyal samurai lands, and in return they promised to fight for him. This relationship is a bit like the one between knights and lords in medieval Europe.

The samurai followed a code of honour, later called [bushidō], "the way of the warrior": loyalty to one's lord, courage, honesty, self-control, and simple living. They trained in archery on horseback, swordsmanship, and later also in poetry and calligraphy.

Sadly, Yoritomo did not trust anyone, not even his own brother Yoshitsune, the hero of the Genpei War. He became jealous of Yoshitsune's popularity and hunted him down. Yoshitsune fled north, but was finally cornered in 1189. Japanese people have always felt sympathy for this tragic hero. There's even an expression, "hōgan-biiki", meaning to feel sorry for the losing side, which comes from his story!

After Yoritomo died in 1199, his wife, Hōjō Masako, and her family, the Hōjō, took control. Masako became known as the "nun shogun". In 1221, when the emperor tried to take back power, she gave a famous speech to the samurai reminding them of everything they owed to Yoritomo. The samurai won, and the Hōjō family ruled for more than 100 years.

title: The Mongol invasions and the 'divine wind'
text:
In the 13th century, the [Mongols], led by Genghis Khan and his descendants, built the largest land empire in history, stretching from Korea to Eastern Europe. Genghis Khan's grandson, Kublai Khan, became emperor of China. He sent letters to Japan asking it to submit and pay tribute. The young regent in Kamakura, Hōjō Tokimune, only 18 years old, refused.

In 1274, Kublai sent an army of about 30,000 soldiers, Mongols, Chinese and Koreans, on 900 ships. They landed in Hakata Bay, in northern Kyushu.

The samurai were surprised. They were used to fighting one-on-one: a warrior would ride forward, announce his name and his family's great deeds, and challenge an enemy. But the Mongols fought in groups, used poisoned arrows, and even bombs that exploded with a loud noise: the first time gunpowder weapons were used against Japan!

The samurai fought bravely. After one day of fighting, the invaders went back to their ships. That night, a storm damaged the fleet, and they sailed home.

The Japanese knew the Mongols would come back. They built a stone wall, about 20 kilometres long and 2 metres high, along Hakata Bay. You can still see parts of it today!

In 1281, Kublai sent an enormous army: about 140,000 soldiers on more than 4,000 ships, one of the largest sea invasions in history before modern times! But thanks to the wall, the invaders could not land easily. The samurai attacked the ships at night in small boats. The fighting went on for weeks.

Then, a powerful [typhoon] struck. Most of the invading fleet was destroyed. The Japanese believed that the gods had sent this storm to protect Japan. They called it the [kamikaze], meaning "divine wind".

However, victory brought problems. Usually, samurai were rewarded with land taken from the enemy. But this time, there was no land to give! Many samurai who had spent their money on the war became poor and angry with the shogunate. This anger helped bring the Kamakura shogunate down in 1333.

Archaeologists have found wrecks of the Mongol ships at the bottom of the sea near Takashima island, with weapons, helmets, and ceramic bombs.

title: New Buddhism for everyone, and the Great Buddha of Kamakura
text:
During the Kamakura period, times were hard. There were wars, earthquakes, famines and fires. Many people believed they were living in the "age of the end of the Law", a dark time when Buddhism would become weak and difficult to practise.

Until then, Buddhism in Japan was mostly for nobles and monks, with complicated rituals and difficult studies. But new teachers appeared who wanted to bring Buddhism to everyone: farmers, warriors, women, poor people.

Hōnen and his student Shinran taught [Pure Land Buddhism]. They said: you don't need to be rich or learned. Just recite with faith the words "Namu Amida Butsu" ("I trust in Amida Buddha"), and Amida Buddha will welcome you into his paradise, the Pure Land, after death. This simple message spread very quickly among ordinary people.

Nichiren taught that the most important thing was a Buddhist text called the Lotus Sutra. He was so outspoken, criticizing other schools and the government, that he was exiled twice!

Monks who had travelled to China brought back [Zen] Buddhism. Zen teaches that you can reach awakening through [meditation], sitting very still and calm, breathing deeply and clearing your mind. The monk Dōgen taught "just sitting". Zen masters also used strange riddles called kōan, like: "What is the sound of one hand clapping?" to help students think differently.

Zen became very popular with the samurai, because it taught discipline, calm in the face of danger, and living in the present moment. Zen also greatly influenced Japanese arts: rock gardens, ink painting, calligraphy, flower arranging, and later the tea ceremony.

The monk Eisai, who brought one school of Zen from China, also brought back tea seeds and wrote a book about the health benefits of drinking tea!

In 1252, the people of Kamakura began building the Great Buddha of Kamakura, a bronze statue of Amida Buddha, 11 metres high. At first, it was inside a wooden hall. But the hall was destroyed by storms and a tsunami in 1498. Since then, the Buddha has been sitting outside, in the open air, calmly meditating under the sky for over 500 years. You can even go inside the statue!

title: The Muromachi shoguns and the Golden Pavilion
text:
In 1333, the Kamakura shogunate collapsed. After a few years of confusion, a samurai named Ashikaga Takauji became shogun in 1338. The Ashikaga shoguns set up their government in Kyoto, in a district called Muromachi. That's why this period is called the Muromachi period (1336–1573).

For about 60 years, there were even two emperors at the same time, one in Kyoto and one in the mountains of Yoshino, each saying he was the true emperor!

The third Ashikaga shogun, Ashikaga Yoshimitsu, put an end to this division in 1392. He was the most powerful of the Ashikaga shoguns. He loved luxury and art, and he traded with China, bringing in silk, books, porcelain and Chinese coins.

In 1397, Yoshimitsu began building a beautiful villa in the north of Kyoto. Its most famous building is a three-storey pavilion. The two upper floors are covered in real gold leaf, and on the roof stands a golden phoenix. It's reflected in a pond surrounded by pine trees and small islands. This is the Kinkaku-ji, the Golden Pavilion. After Yoshimitsu's death, the villa became a Zen temple.

Sadly, in 1950, a young monk set fire to the Golden Pavilion, and it burned down. It was rebuilt exactly as it was in 1955, and in 1987 it was covered with new gold leaf, even thicker than before! It's one of the most visited places in Japan.

About 90 years later, another shogun, Ashikaga Yoshimasa, built a villa in the east of Kyoto, inspired by his grandfather's. Its main building is called the Ginkaku-ji, the Silver Pavilion... even though it was never covered in silver! It has a much simpler, calmer beauty, with a garden of white sand shaped like waves.

The Muromachi period saw the birth of many arts that are still considered very Japanese today: ikebana (flower arranging), Zen rock gardens, ink painting, the tea ceremony, and Noh theatre. A new style of room also appeared, with tatami mats covering the whole floor, sliding doors, and a special alcove, called tokonoma, to display a scroll or flowers. Many Japanese homes still have one today!

title: Zeami and Noh theatre
text:
Imagine a theatre where the actors move incredibly slowly, wear beautiful carved wooden masks, and the stage has only a painted pine tree in the background. Welcome to Noh, the oldest form of theatre in the world that is still performed today!

Noh developed from popular performances with music, dance, acrobatics and comedy performed at shrines and temples. In the 14th century, an actor named Kan'ami and especially his son, Zeami, transformed it into a refined art.

In 1374, the young shogun Ashikaga Yoshimitsu watched a performance by Kan'ami and his 11-year-old son Zeami. He was so impressed by the handsome boy's talent that he took them under his protection. With the shogun's support, Zeami became the greatest Noh actor and playwright of all time. He wrote around 50 plays that are still performed!

Zeami also wrote books explaining his art. He talked about [yūgen], a mysterious, deep and subtle beauty, like the moon hidden behind thin clouds. He wrote: "What is hidden is flower", meaning that what is suggested is more powerful than what is shown.

In Noh, the main character often wears a [Noh mask]. There are masks of young women, old men, demons, and ghosts. They are carved so cleverly that by tilting the mask slightly up or down, the actor can make it look happy or sad! Many Noh plays are about ghosts who come back to tell their story and find peace.

The actors are accompanied by a chorus and musicians playing a flute and drums. The musicians also shout strange cries like "Yoooo!" and "Ha!" to mark the rhythm.

The stage is special: it is square, made of polished cypress wood, with a roof, even when it's indoors! A long bridge on the side, called the hashigakari, lets actors enter as if coming from another world.

Between two serious Noh plays, actors perform [kyōgen], short funny plays with clever servants who trick their masters. It's the comedy of old Japan!

Noh has been performed for more than 600 years, and it is listed by UNESCO as an [Intangible Cultural Heritage] of humanity.

title: The Ryukyu Kingdom, bridge of the seas
text:
Far to the south of Japan's main islands lies a chain of subtropical islands with white beaches, coral reefs and turquoise sea: the [Ryukyu Islands], with Okinawa as the largest. For a long time, they were not part of Japan. They were an independent kingdom with its own culture, language and kings!

In the 14th century, Okinawa island was divided into three small kingdoms, often at war. In 1429, a king named Shō Hashi united them and founded the Ryukyu Kingdom. Its capital was Shuri, where kings lived in a magnificent red castle: Shuri Castle.

The Ryukyu Kingdom had very few natural resources, but it had a great location, right in the middle of the seas between Japan, China, Korea and Southeast Asia. So the people of Ryukyu became great sailors and traders! Their ships sailed to China, Japan, Korea, Thailand, Java and Malacca. They bought and sold silk, porcelain, swords, spices, sappanwood for dye, and horses. The kingdom became rich thanks to trade.

A big bell made in 1458 for Shuri Castle is inscribed with the words: "Ryukyu is a bridge between all nations."

Ryukyu had close ties with China. Chinese envoys visited to confirm each new king. Ryukyu culture mixed Chinese, Japanese and Southeast Asian influences with its own traditions. Many things we know today come from Ryukyu: the martial art of [karate], the three-stringed instrument called [sanshin], colourful textiles called bingata, and the lion-dog guardians called shīsā that you still see on Okinawan roofs!

In 1609, the Satsuma domain from southern Kyushu invaded Ryukyu. The kingdom still existed but had to obey Satsuma and pay it taxes, while still sending tribute to China.

In 1879, the Japanese government put an end to the kingdom. The last king was forced to move to Tokyo, and Ryukyu became [Okinawa Prefecture].

Shuri Castle was destroyed during World War II in 1945, rebuilt in 1992, and sadly burned down again in 2019. It is being rebuilt once more, with the hope of finishing in 2026. The people of Okinawa are very proud of their unique history and culture.

title: The Ōnin War and the Warring States period
text:
In 1467, a terrible war broke out in Kyoto. It started with a quarrel about who would be the next shogun, and which family would lead two powerful samurai clans. The great lords of Japan took sides: one group camped in the east of Kyoto, the other in the west.

This was the Ōnin War. It lasted 11 years, until 1477. Most of the fighting took place in the streets of Kyoto itself. The beautiful capital was burned and destroyed. Temples, palaces and houses went up in flames. People said you could see the sky from anywhere in the city because nothing was left standing.

Even today, some people in Kyoto jokingly say "before the war" to mean before the Ōnin War, not World War II!

In the end, nobody really won. But the shogun lost almost all his power. From then on, Japan fell into more than 100 years of chaos called the Sengoku period, the "Warring States period".

Japan was divided among dozens of powerful warlords called [daimyō]. Each daimyō ruled his own territory like a small kingdom, with his own army, castle and laws, and tried to conquer his neighbours.

It was a time of [gekokujō], "the low overthrowing the high". Servants betrayed their masters, and ordinary warriors, even farmers, could become great lords if they were clever and strong enough. Many famous daimyō started from very humble beginnings.

To protect themselves, the daimyō built castles on hilltops, and later great castles with stone walls and tall towers. Around the castles, towns grew up, with merchants and craftsmen. Many Japanese cities today began as castle towns.

The Warring States period was violent, but it was also a time of change and energy. Trade grew, new mines were opened, and new ideas spread. Some famous warlords from this time, like Takeda Shingen and Uesugi Kenshin, who fought each other five times at Kawanakajima, are still heroes of films, manga and video games today.

Many people wondered: who will finally bring peace and unite Japan? The answer would come in three men: Nobunaga, Hideyoshi and Ieyasu.

title: Portuguese sailors bring guns to Tanegashima
text:
In 1543, a Chinese ship was blown off course by a storm and landed on Tanegashima, a small island south of Kyushu. On board were two or three Portuguese traders: the first Europeans ever to set foot in Japan!

The young lord of the island, Tanegashima Tokitaka, only 15 years old, was fascinated by something the Portuguese carried: long guns called [arquebuses]. He watched them shoot a duck from far away and was amazed. He bought two of them for a huge sum of money.

Then he asked his swordsmith, Yaita Kinbei, to make copies. It was very difficult! The hardest part was the screw at the back of the barrel: the Japanese had never made screws before. A legend says the swordsmith's daughter, Wakasa, married a Portuguese sailor to learn the secret... Whether it's true or not, within a year, Japanese craftsmen were making their own guns.

In Japan, these guns were called "tanegashima", after the island. Japanese smiths quickly made them better, and produced them in large numbers in towns like Sakai and Kunitomo. Within a few decades, Japan probably had more guns than any country in Europe!

Guns changed the way wars were fought in the Warring States period. Until then, the most admired warriors were brave samurai on horseback with swords and bows. Now, a simple foot soldier with a gun could defeat a skilled samurai from a distance. Armies needed thousands of [ashigaru], foot soldiers armed with guns and long spears.

Castles also changed: they needed thick stone walls to resist bullets.

The warlord who understood this best was Oda Nobunaga. In 1575, at the Battle of Nagashino, he placed about 3,000 gunmen behind wooden fences, firing in turns. They defeated the famous cavalry of the Takeda clan.

The Portuguese also brought other things to Japan: bread (pan in Japanese comes from Portuguese pão!), tempura, a sponge cake called castella, playing cards, and tobacco.

Today, Tanegashima is famous for something else: it has Japan's main space centre, from which rockets are launched into space!

title: Francis Xavier and the 'southern barbarians'
text:
In 1549, a Spanish [Jesuit] priest named Francis Xavier landed in Kagoshima, in southern Kyushu. He was the first Christian missionary in Japan.

Xavier admired the Japanese. He wrote that they were "the best people yet discovered", very curious, polite, and concerned with honour. He travelled to Kyoto hoping to meet the emperor, but the capital was in ruins because of the wars, and he couldn't. He left Japan after two years, but other missionaries followed him.

The Portuguese came to Japan every year on huge ships called "black ships" because of their dark hulls. The Japanese called the Europeans "[nanban]", meaning "southern barbarians", because they arrived from the south. This trade is called the nanban trade.

The Portuguese brought Chinese silk, guns, glass, clocks, eyeglasses and maps. They took back Japanese silver, swords and lacquerware. Japanese artists painted beautiful folding screens called nanban screens, showing tall Europeans with baggy trousers, big hats and long noses, along with their ships and even their exotic animals!

Some daimyō became Christians. They were called "Christian daimyō". Some were sincere believers, others were also interested in trade and guns. Christianity spread quickly, especially in Kyushu. By around 1600, there were perhaps 300,000 Japanese Christians, called [Kirishitan].

In 1582, four young Japanese boys, about 13 years old, were sent to Europe: the Tenshō embassy. They travelled for more than two years, met the King of Spain and the Pope in Rome, and were welcomed like princes! When they came back eight years later, they brought a printing press.

But the rulers of Japan began to fear that Christianity was a way for European countries to take over Japan, as they had done in the Americas and the Philippines. In 1597, 26 Christians, Japanese and European, were crucified in Nagasaki. In 1614, Christianity was banned completely. Missionaries were expelled, and Christians were persecuted.

Some Japanese Christians kept their faith in secret for more than 250 years. They were called [hidden Christians]. They disguised statues of Mary as Kannon, a Buddhist goddess of mercy, and passed down prayers in a mix of Latin, Portuguese and Japanese!

title: Oda Nobunaga, the first unifier
text:
Oda Nobunaga was the son of a small lord in Owari province, near today's Nagoya. As a teenager, he was so wild and strange that people called him "the fool of Owari"! He wore messy clothes, ate while walking in the street, and hung out with village boys.

But he proved everyone wrong. In 1560, at the Battle of Okehazama, Nobunaga, with only about 2,000 to 3,000 soldiers, attacked the army of the powerful warlord Imagawa Yoshimoto, who had around 25,000 men. Nobunaga launched a surprise attack during a heavy rainstorm, while the Imagawa army was resting and celebrating, and killed Yoshimoto. Suddenly, Nobunaga was famous!

Nobunaga's goal was clear. His seal carried the words "tenka fubu", which can mean "rule the whole country by military force". Step by step, he conquered central Japan. In 1568, he entered Kyoto and installed a shogun who obeyed him. A few years later, he drove that shogun out, ending the Muromachi shogunate.

Nobunaga was very modern for his time. He used guns on a large scale. He encouraged trade by creating "free markets" where anyone could sell without paying fees. He was curious about European things, and welcomed the missionaries. He even had an African servant named Yasuke, who became a samurai!

But he could also be extremely cruel. He burned the great Buddhist temple complex of Mount Hiei near Kyoto in 1571, killing thousands of monks and people, because the monks had sided with his enemies.

He built a magnificent castle at Azuchi, on the shore of Lake Biwa, with a seven-storey tower decorated with gold and paintings. It was one of the first great Japanese castles.

In 1582, when Nobunaga was close to controlling half of Japan, he stayed in a temple in Kyoto called Honnō-ji with only a few guards. One of his own generals, Akechi Mitsuhide, suddenly betrayed him and attacked the temple. Surrounded, Nobunaga set the temple on fire and took his own life. He was 48. Why did Mitsuhide betray him? It's still one of the great mysteries of Japanese history!

title: Toyotomi Hideyoshi unifies Japan
text:
Toyotomi Hideyoshi's life is an incredible story: he started at the very bottom and rose to the very top!

He was born in 1537 in a poor farming family. He was small and thin, and people nicknamed him "monkey". As a young man, he became a sandal-bearer for Oda Nobunaga. A famous story says that on a cold winter day, he kept his master's sandals warm inside his own clothes. Nobunaga noticed his cleverness, and Hideyoshi rose quickly to become one of his best generals.

When Nobunaga was betrayed in 1582, Hideyoshi was far away, fighting in the west. He made peace with his enemy in a hurry and marched his army about 200 kilometres back to Kyoto in only about ten days. He defeated the traitor Akechi Mitsuhide. Then he took over Nobunaga's work.

By 1590, after defeating the last great lords who resisted, Hideyoshi had [unified] all of Japan. After more than 100 years of civil war, the country was finally under one ruler! Because he was not from a noble family, he could not become shogun, but the emperor gave him the highest titles at court.

To keep the peace, he made important changes:
- The [sword hunt] of 1588: farmers had to hand over all their swords and weapons. Only samurai could be armed.
- He fixed the classes of society: samurai could not become farmers or merchants, and farmers could not become samurai. (Ironic, since he had been a farmer's son himself!)
- He measured all the rice fields of Japan to calculate taxes fairly.

He built the enormous Osaka Castle, the greatest castle of its time, with a tower covered in gold. He loved gold so much that he had a golden tea room that could be taken apart and carried!

But Hideyoshi's ambitions went too far. He wanted to conquer China. In 1592 and 1597, he sent huge armies to invade [Korea]. The wars were a disaster. The Korean admiral Yi Sun-sin defeated the Japanese navy with his famous "turtle ships". Hundreds of thousands of Koreans died, and the country was devastated. This war left a very painful memory in Korea.

Hideyoshi died in 1598. His son was only 5 years old...

title: The Battle of Sekigahara
text:
Before he died, Hideyoshi asked five great lords to protect his young son, Hideyori, until he grew up. The most powerful of them was Tokugawa Ieyasu.

Ieyasu had had a hard life. As a child, he was sent as a hostage to other families for years. He had been an ally of Nobunaga and then of Hideyoshi. He was known for his patience. A famous saying compares the three unifiers: if a bird, a little cuckoo, won't sing, Nobunaga says: "I'll kill it!" Hideyoshi says: "I'll make it want to sing." Ieyasu says: "I'll wait until it sings."

After Hideyoshi's death, Ieyasu stopped waiting. He began acting as if he were the ruler of Japan. Other lords, led by Ishida Mitsunari, a loyal servant of the Toyotomi family, opposed him.

Japan split into two camps: the Eastern Army of Ieyasu and the Western Army of Mitsunari. On the 21st of October 1600, about 160,000 samurai met in a narrow mountain valley called Sekigahara, in the middle of Japan. It was one of the largest battles in Japanese history.

The day began in thick fog. When it lifted, the two armies clashed. For hours, the Western Army resisted. But Ieyasu had secretly convinced several Western lords to change sides. The most important was a young lord named Kobayakawa Hideaki, who hesitated on a hill for a long time. Legend says Ieyasu ordered his gunners to fire toward Kobayakawa's hill to push him to make up his mind! Finally, Kobayakawa attacked his own allies. The Western Army collapsed. The battle was over in about six hours.

Ieyasu was now the master of Japan. Japanese people still say "Sekigahara" to describe a decisive moment, like a final exam or a big game!

But Hideyori, Hideyoshi's son, was still living in the great Osaka Castle. In 1614 and 1615, Ieyasu attacked it in the Siege of Osaka. The castle burned, and Hideyori and his mother took their own lives. The Toyotomi family was gone.

Ieyasu could now build a government that would last for more than 250 years.

title: Tokugawa Ieyasu founds the Edo shogunate
text:
In 1603, the emperor gave Tokugawa Ieyasu the title of shogun. Ieyasu did not set up his government in Kyoto, but in his own castle town far to the east: [Edo], a small fishing village surrounded by marshes. Today, it's called... Tokyo!

This began the Edo period, which lasted from 1603 to 1868: 265 years of peace, with 15 Tokugawa shoguns. Japan had never known such a long peace!

Ieyasu gave the shogun title to his son only two years later, so that everyone understood that the Tokugawa family would keep it forever. But he continued to rule behind the scenes until his death in 1616. He was then honoured as a god at the magnificent Nikkō Tōshō-gū shrine, famous for its carvings of three wise monkeys: "see no evil, hear no evil, speak no evil"!

To make sure no one could ever challenge them, the Tokugawa set up a very strict system. Japan was divided into about 260 domains ruled by daimyō. The daimyō closest to the Tokugawa received land near Edo; the ones who had been enemies at Sekigahara were sent far away. Daimyō were not allowed to build new castles or marry without permission.

Society was divided into four main classes:
- samurai, at the top, who served as warriors and officials,
- farmers, who were respected because they produced rice,
- craftsmen,
- merchants, who were at the bottom, because they were thought only to make money without producing anything.

In reality, many merchants became very rich, and many samurai became poor! Outside these classes, there were also people who were discriminated against, doing jobs considered "unclean".

During the long peace, samurai had fewer and fewer wars to fight. They became administrators, teachers, and scholars. Schools spread, even for children of farmers and merchants, called [terakoya]. By the end of the Edo period, Japan had one of the highest literacy rates in the world!

Edo grew enormously. By 1700, it had about one million people, making it one of the largest cities in the world, bigger than London or Paris at the time.

title: Sankin-kōtai: the great processions of the lords
text:
How can you stop 260 powerful lords from rebelling against you? The Tokugawa shoguns found a clever answer.

In 1635, the third shogun, Tokugawa Iemitsu, made official a system called sankin-kōtai, which means "alternate attendance". Every daimyō had to live in Edo every other year, near the shogun. And when they returned to their domain, they had to leave their wife and eldest son in Edo, as a kind of polite hostage!

Travelling between their domain and Edo was very expensive. A daimyō had to travel with a huge procession: samurai, servants, porters, horses, carrying luggage, weapons and gifts. The biggest processions, like that of the Kaga domain, had more than 2,000 people! The daimyō also had to maintain big mansions in Edo. This cost so much money that the daimyō had little left to raise an army against the shogun. Clever, isn't it?

The processions were a real show. When a daimyō's procession passed, ordinary people had to kneel by the roadside and bow until it had gone by. At the front, men shouted "Shita ni! Shita ni!", meaning "Down! Down!"

These journeys used a network of great roads called the [Five Routes]. The most famous was the Tōkaidō, the "Eastern Sea Road", between Edo and Kyoto, along the Pacific coast. It had 53 post stations, towns where travellers could eat, rest and change horses. At the station towns, there were inns, restaurants, tea houses and souvenir shops.

Many ordinary people also travelled, especially on [pilgrimages] to famous shrines like Ise. Travelling became so popular that guidebooks were sold! A comic novel told the adventures of two funny travellers on the Tōkaidō and was a huge bestseller.

The artist Hiroshige made a famous series of prints called "The Fifty-three Stations of the Tōkaidō", showing each station in the rain, snow, or sunset.

The sankin-kōtai system had an unexpected result: it helped unite Japan. Money, goods, fashions, food and ideas travelled along the roads between Edo and the provinces. Edo became a place where people from all over Japan met, and a common culture spread across the country.

title: Sakoku: Japan closes its doors
text:
In the early Edo period, the Tokugawa became more and more suspicious of foreigners, especially Christian missionaries. They feared that European countries would use Christianity to take over Japan.

In 1637, a big rebellion broke out in Shimabara, near Nagasaki. Poor farmers, many of them Christians, rose up against the heavy taxes and cruelty of their lord. They were led by a charismatic teenager, only 16 years old, named Amakusa Shirō. About 37,000 rebels held out in an old castle for months, but they were finally crushed, and almost all were killed.

After this Shimabara Rebellion, the shogunate decided to close Japan. In 1639, Portuguese ships were banned. This policy was later called sakoku, "closed country".

- Japanese people were not allowed to leave Japan. Those who were abroad could not come back, under penalty of death!
- Christianity was strictly forbidden. People had to register at Buddhist temples. Some were even forced to step on pictures of Jesus or Mary, called fumi-e, to prove they were not Christians.
- Foreign trade was strictly controlled.

But Japan was not completely closed. It kept four "windows" to the world: trade with China and the Netherlands at Nagasaki, with Korea through the Tsushima domain, with the Ryukyu Kingdom through Satsuma, and with the Ainu people through the Matsumae domain in the north.

The Dutch were allowed to stay because they were Protestants and only interested in trade, not in spreading religion. But they had to live on Dejima, a small fan-shaped artificial island in Nagasaki harbour, about as big as two football fields! They could not leave without permission. Once a year, the Dutch chief had to travel to Edo to bring gifts to the shogun.

Through Dejima, Japan continued to learn about Western science. Japanese scholars studied Dutch books on medicine, astronomy, geography and botany. This was called rangaku, "Dutch learning". In 1774, a group of doctors translated a Dutch anatomy book into Japanese after comparing its drawings with a real human body. They were amazed to see how accurate it was!

Sakoku lasted for more than 200 years, until 1854.

title: Bashō, kabuki and the joys of Edo culture
text:
During the long Edo peace, cities like Edo, Osaka and Kyoto grew rich. Merchants and townspeople had money and free time, and they wanted to have fun! A lively new culture was born, especially during the [Genroku era] (around 1688–1704).

The greatest poet of this time was Matsuo Bashō. He was a master of short poems that we now call [haiku]. A haiku has only 17 syllables, in three lines of 5, 7 and 5 syllables. It usually captures a small moment in nature and includes a word that shows the season.

His most famous haiku goes like this:
"An old silent pond... / A frog jumps into the pond— / Splash! Silence again."
Just a frog and a sound, but it makes you feel the quiet of the place!

In 1689, Bashō set off on foot with a friend on a journey of about 2,400 kilometres through northern Japan. He wrote about it in a famous travel diary called "The Narrow Road to the Deep North", mixing prose and haiku. Today, Japanese children learn his poems at school, and people all over the world write haiku in their own languages.

In the cities, people loved the theatre. [Kabuki] was a spectacular, colourful theatre with dramatic stories, dazzling costumes, bold make-up, and stage tricks like trapdoors and revolving stages! Kabuki was started around 1603 by a woman named Izumo no Okuni, but women were later banned from performing, so all roles, including women's, were played by men. Kabuki is still performed today.

Another popular art was [bunraku], puppet theatre. Each large puppet is moved by three puppeteers dressed in black, while a narrator tells the story and a musician plays the shamisen. The great playwright Chikamatsu Monzaemon wrote plays for both bunraku and kabuki, about love, honour and ordinary people's lives.

People also enjoyed sumo wrestling, fireworks over the Sumida River, reading illustrated books, and eating at street stalls. Some of Japan's favourite foods, like [sushi], tempura and soba noodles, became popular as fast food in Edo!

This joyful urban world was called the [ukiyo], the "floating world", a world of pleasure and passing moments.

title: Inō Tadataka walks across Japan to map it
text:
Here's an amazing story for anyone who thinks it's too late to start something new!

Inō Tadataka was born in 1745. He was adopted into a family of rich merchants in a town near Edo, and ran their business successfully for many years. But he had always loved astronomy and mathematics.

At the age of 50, when most people at that time were thinking about retiring, he handed over the business to his son, moved to Edo, and became a student of a young astronomer, 19 years younger than him! He studied very hard, observing the stars day and night.

Tadataka wanted to calculate the size of the Earth. To do that, he needed to measure a long distance on the ground very precisely. So he proposed to the shogunate to make a map of Hokkaido, then called Ezo. At that time, foreign ships, especially Russian ones, were appearing in the north, and the government needed good maps.

In 1800, at the age of 55, he set out. He measured distances by walking with a very regular step, about 69 centimetres per step, and using ropes and chains. At night, he observed the stars to calculate his exact position. It was hard work, in all weathers, over mountains and along rocky coasts.

His first map was so good that the shogunate asked him to continue. For 17 years, he and his team travelled all around Japan. In total, they walked about 40,000 kilometres, about the distance around the whole Earth!

Tadataka died in 1818, before the map was finished. His students completed it in 1821. It was called the Dai Nihon Enkai Yochi Zenzu, "Maps of the Coastal Regions of Great Japan", and it was incredibly accurate. When British sailors saw a copy decades later, they were so impressed they decided they didn't need to map the Japanese coast themselves!

And the size of the Earth? Tadataka's calculation was very close to the real value, less than 0.1% off!

Today, Inō Tadataka is a symbol of the idea that it's never too late to learn. There is a museum about him in his hometown of Sawara, in Chiba.

title: Hokusai and The Great Wave
text:
You have probably seen this picture before: a gigantic blue wave, with claw-like foam, about to crash onto three small boats, and in the background, tiny Mount Fuji. It's "The Great Wave off Kanagawa", one of the most famous images in the world. It was made around 1831 by the artist Katsushika Hokusai.

The Great Wave is a [woodblock print], a type of art called [ukiyo-e], "pictures of the floating world". To make one, several craftsmen worked together. The artist drew the picture. A carver cut it into blocks of cherry wood, one block for each colour. Then a printer put ink on each block and pressed paper onto them, one after the other. This way, hundreds of copies could be made and sold cheaply, like posters. Ordinary people in Edo could buy them for about the price of a bowl of noodles!

Ukiyo-e showed popular subjects: kabuki actors, beautiful women, sumo wrestlers, landscapes, legends and ghosts.

The Great Wave is part of a series called "Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji". It used a new imported pigment, [Prussian blue], a bright, strong blue that became very fashionable.

Hokusai was a fascinating character. He lived to almost 90 and made about 30,000 artworks! He changed his name more than 30 times and moved house 93 times, some say because he never cleaned his home, and moved when it got too messy! He also published books of sketches called "Hokusai Manga", full of people, animals and funny faces. They are one of the ancestors of modern manga.

Near the end of his life, he wrote: "At 73, I began to understand the true form of animals, insects and fish. At 90, I will know their secret. At 100, I will be divine. If heaven gave me five more years, I could become a true painter!"

Another great ukiyo-e artist of this time was Hiroshige, famous for his landscapes of rain and snow.

When Japan opened to the world in the 1850s, ukiyo-e prints arrived in Europe, sometimes as wrapping paper for porcelain! European artists like Van Gogh, Monet and Degas were amazed. Van Gogh even copied some Japanese prints. This fashion for Japanese art was called [Japonisme]. Today, The Great Wave appears on Japanese passports and on the 1,000-yen banknote!

title: Commodore Perry's black ships
text:
On the 8th of July 1853, the people of Uraga, near Edo, saw something terrifying: four huge black ships entering the bay, belching smoke! Two of them were [steamships] that could move without wind. The Japanese called them the black ships.

They were American warships commanded by Commodore Matthew Perry. He carried a letter from the President of the United States. The Americans wanted Japan to open its ports so that their ships, especially whaling ships in the Pacific, could get coal, water and food, and to start trading.

Perry refused to go to Nagasaki, the only port where foreigners were allowed. He showed off his cannons and demanded that the letter be accepted. The shogunate was in shock. After more than 200 years of peace and closed borders, Japan's old cannons and samurai were no match for modern warships. The shogun's officials accepted the letter, and Perry said he would return for an answer.

In 1854, Perry came back with nine ships. The shogunate had no choice. It signed the Convention of Kanagawa, opening two ports, Shimoda and Hakodate, to American ships. Perry brought gifts to show American technology: a small steam train that ran on a circular track, and a telegraph! The Japanese gave gifts too, and sumo wrestlers showed their strength by carrying heavy bags of rice.

A few years later, Japan signed trade treaties with the United States, Britain, France, the Netherlands and Russia. But these treaties were [unequal treaties]: foreigners in Japan could not be judged by Japanese courts, and Japan could not set its own customs taxes. Many Japanese felt humiliated.

A popular joke poem at the time said: "The tea called Jōkisen woke us from our peaceful sleep; with only four cups, we can't sleep at night!" It was a pun: "jōkisen" means both a kind of tea and "steamship".

The country was thrown into turmoil. Many samurai were furious with the shogunate for giving in. They shouted the slogan "[Sonnō jōi]!": "Revere the emperor, expel the barbarians!" Some attacked foreigners. The years of chaos that followed are called the [Bakumatsu], "the end of the shogunate". Young samurai, like the famous Sakamoto Ryōma, began to dream of a new Japan.

title: The Meiji Restoration
text:
In the 1860s, powerful domains in western Japan, especially [Satsuma] (in southern Kyushu) and [Chōshū] (at the western tip of Honshu), decided that the shogunate was too weak to protect Japan from foreign countries. They joined forces to overthrow it. The young samurai Sakamoto Ryōma helped bring these two former rivals together.

In 1867, the last shogun, Tokugawa Yoshinobu, gave power back to the emperor. In January 1868, the emperor's supporters officially announced the "restoration of imperial rule". This is called the Meiji Restoration. Some supporters of the shogunate fought back in a civil war called the Boshin War, but they were defeated in 1869.

The emperor at that time was a teenager, only 15 years old: Emperor Meiji. His era name "Meiji" means "enlightened rule". The capital moved from Kyoto to Edo, which was renamed [Tokyo], "Eastern Capital". The emperor moved into the old shogun's castle, which became the Imperial Palace.

In 1868, the new government announced its goals in the Charter Oath. It promised that decisions would be made after public discussion and that "knowledge shall be sought throughout the world".

In reality, power was held by a group of young leaders, mostly former samurai from Satsuma and Chōshū, like Ōkubo Toshimichi, Saigō Takamori and Itō Hirobumi. Their slogan was "Fukoku kyōhei": "Rich country, strong army". They wanted Japan to become modern very fast, to be strong enough never to be dominated by Western countries.

The changes were enormous:
- The domains were abolished in 1871 and replaced by prefectures, like today.
- The four social classes were abolished. Samurai lost their privileges, and in 1876 they were even forbidden to wear swords in public!
- Everyone could now choose their job and have a family name.
- A modern army was created, with young men of all classes called up for military service.

Not everyone was happy. In 1877, some unhappy former samurai rebelled in Satsuma, led by Saigō Takamori, one of the heroes of the Restoration. This was the Satsuma Rebellion. The new army defeated them. Saigō died, and he became a tragic hero. His statue, with his dog, stands in Ueno Park in Tokyo. It was the end of the samurai.

title: Hokkaido and the Ainu people
text:
The northern island of Japan, Hokkaido, is a land of snowy mountains, forests, bears and salmon rivers. For centuries, it was not the home of Japanese people, but of another people: the Ainu.

The Ainu are an [Indigenous people] who have lived in Hokkaido, the southern Kuril Islands and southern Sakhalin for a very long time. They have their own language, the Ainu language, which is completely different from Japanese, and their own religion and traditions.

The Ainu lived by hunting deer and bears, fishing for salmon, and gathering plants. They believed that everything in nature, animals, plants, fire, water, tools, has a spirit, called a [kamuy]. When they hunted an animal, they thanked its spirit and sent it back to the world of the gods with respect. They were known for their beautiful clothing decorated with swirling patterns, and for their long spoken stories and songs, called yukar, passed down from memory.

During the Edo period, a Japanese domain called Matsumae controlled trade with the Ainu. The trade was often unfair, and the Ainu were exploited. They rebelled several times, notably under the leader Shakushain in 1669, but were defeated.

In 1869, after the Meiji Restoration, the Japanese government officially took over the island, which the Japanese called Ezo, and renamed it Hokkaido. Many Japanese settlers were sent there to farm, build towns and railways, and protect the north from Russia. The city of Sapporo was built.

For the Ainu, it was a very hard time. Their lands were taken. They were forbidden to hunt deer and fish salmon in their traditional way. They were forced to take Japanese names, and children were taught only in Japanese. Their language and culture almost disappeared. Ainu people often faced discrimination.

But the Ainu kept fighting for their rights and their culture. In 2019, a Japanese law officially recognized the Ainu as an Indigenous people of Japan. In 2020, a national museum and park called Upopoy, meaning "singing together" in Ainu, opened in Hokkaido to celebrate and revive Ainu culture.

Many place names in Hokkaido come from the Ainu language. Even "Sapporo" probably comes from Ainu words meaning "big dry river"!

title: Trains, schools and silk: Japan modernizes
text:
In 1871, a large group of Japanese leaders set off on a long journey around the world: the Iwakura Mission. For almost two years, they visited the United States and Europe, looking at factories, schools, parliaments, railways, museums and armies. They were amazed, and they decided: Japan must catch up, fast!

What happened next is one of the fastest transformations of any country in history.

In 1872, Japan's first railway opened, between Shimbashi in Tokyo and Yokohama, 29 kilometres long. The engines came from Britain. People were so unused to trains that some of the first passengers took off their shoes before getting on, as if entering a house, and were surprised to find them left behind on the platform!

The same year, the government created a modern [school system]. Education became compulsory for all children, boys and girls. By 1900, almost all Japanese children went to primary school.

Also in 1872, Japan switched from the lunar calendar to the Western solar calendar. The 3rd of December suddenly became the 1st of January 1873!

The government built modern factories. The most famous is the Tomioka Silk Mill, opened in 1872 with French machines and French engineers. Hundreds of young women, many of them daughters of former samurai, came to learn to reel silk and then taught others. Silk became Japan's most important export. The mill is now a UNESCO World Heritage site.

Western things became fashionable: people began to wear Western clothes, cut their hair short, eat beef and bread, and build brick buildings. Gas lamps lit the streets of Tokyo's Ginza district. This fashion was called "bunmei kaika", "civilization and enlightenment".

The writer [Fukuzawa Yukichi] encouraged Japanese people to learn and think for themselves. His book "An Encouragement of Learning" begins: "Heaven does not create one person above another, nor one person below another." It was a bestseller. His face is on the old 10,000-yen banknote!

In just about 40 years, Japan went from a country of samurai and ox-carts to a modern industrial nation with railways, factories, steamships, telegraphs and newspapers.

title: The Meiji Constitution and Japan's first parliament
text:
After the Meiji Restoration, many Japanese people wanted a bigger say in how their country was run. In the 1870s and 1880s, a movement called the Freedom and People's Rights Movement spread across Japan. Its members held meetings, wrote petitions and newspapers, and demanded a constitution and an elected parliament. Some people even wrote their own draft constitutions!

The government agreed to create a constitution, but it wanted to keep strong control. Itō Hirobumi, one of the main leaders, travelled to Europe to study different constitutions. He especially liked the one of Germany, where the emperor had a lot of power.

On the 11th of February 1889, the Meiji Constitution was proclaimed. It was the first modern constitution in Asia! Japan now had a [parliament], called the Imperial Diet, with two houses: a House of Peers, made up of nobles and people chosen by the emperor, and a House of Representatives, elected by the people.

The first elections took place in 1890. But only a very small number of people could vote: men over 25 who paid a lot of taxes. That was only about 1% of the population! Women could not vote at all.

In the Meiji Constitution, the emperor was described as "sacred and inviolable". He was the head of state and the commander of the army and navy. In theory, he had enormous power, but in practice, government leaders made most decisions in his name.

Itō Hirobumi became the first [Prime Minister] of Japan in 1885. He is also remembered for having been on the old 1,000-yen banknote.

The government also wanted to build national unity around the emperor. In 1890, it issued the Imperial Rescript on Education, which schoolchildren had to learn by heart. It taught loyalty to the emperor and love of the country, along with values like respecting parents and studying hard.

Having a modern constitution and parliament also helped Japan prove to Western countries that it was a "civilized" modern nation. Little by little, Japan managed to get rid of the unequal treaties. By 1911, Japan had fully regained control over its own laws and customs taxes.

title: Wars with China and Russia, and an empire
text:
At the end of the 19th century, the powerful countries of Europe and the United States were creating [colonial empires] across Asia and Africa. Japan's leaders feared that Japan could also be colonized. They decided that Japan, too, should become a great power... with its own empire. Sadly, this meant doing to its neighbours what Western countries had done elsewhere.

The first conflict was about Korea. Both Japan and China wanted influence over Korea. In 1894–1895, they fought the First Sino-Japanese War. Japan's modern army and navy won easily. China had to give Japan the island of [Taiwan], which became a Japanese colony for 50 years.

Then Japan clashed with Russia, which wanted to expand into Manchuria and Korea. In 1904–1905, Japan and Russia fought the Russo-Japanese War. It was very bloody. At Port Arthur and Mukden, tens of thousands of soldiers died. At sea, in 1905, Admiral Tōgō Heihachirō destroyed the Russian fleet, which had sailed all the way from Europe, at the Battle of Tsushima.

The whole world was astonished. For the first time in modern history, an Asian country had defeated a European great power! Some people in other Asian countries, colonized by Europeans, were inspired by Japan's victory. The peace treaty was signed in the United States, thanks to President Theodore Roosevelt, who received the Nobel Peace Prize for it.

But many Japanese people were angry that the treaty did not give Japan more, and riots broke out in Tokyo.

After the war, Japan took more and more control of Korea. In 1910, Japan [annexed] Korea, making it a colony. For the Korean people, this was a tragedy. For 35 years, until 1945, Koreans lived under Japanese rule. Their land was taken, they were pushed to use the Japanese language and later to take Japanese names, and many who resisted were imprisoned. Koreans remember this period with great pain, and it still affects relations between the two countries today.

In 1912, Emperor Meiji died. In less than 50 years, Japan had gone from a closed country to a world power with an empire. His son became emperor, beginning the [Taishō] era.

title: The Great Kantō Earthquake
text:
The [Taishō era] (1912–1926) was a lively time. Japan became richer thanks to World War I, in which it fought on the side of Britain and France. Cities grew. In Tokyo and Osaka, people went to cafés, cinemas, department stores and baseball games. Young women with short hair and Western dresses, called "modern girls", walked the streets. Many people demanded more democracy, and in 1925, all men over 25 got the right to vote. This period is sometimes called Taishō democracy.

But on the 1st of September 1923, at 11:58 in the morning, disaster struck. A huge [earthquake] of magnitude 7.9 shook the Kantō region, where Tokyo and Yokohama are. The ground shook for several minutes.

It was almost lunchtime, and in many homes people were cooking on fires. Most houses were made of wood. Fires broke out everywhere, and strong winds from a typhoon spread them quickly. In some places, the fires created terrible [fire whirlwinds], like tornadoes of flame. Much of Tokyo and Yokohama burned for two days.

More than 100,000 people died. It was one of the worst disasters in Japanese history.

In the chaos, false rumours spread that Koreans living in Japan were poisoning wells and starting fires. Groups of people, and even some soldiers and police, attacked and killed thousands of Koreans and also some Chinese and Japanese people. It's a shameful and sad chapter that reminds us how dangerous rumours and prejudice can be, especially in times of fear.

Tokyo was rebuilt with wider streets, parks, and more concrete buildings to resist earthquakes and fires. Many modern bridges over the Sumida River date from this reconstruction.

Japan is located where four [tectonic plates] meet, so earthquakes happen very often. Since 1960, the 1st of September has been Disaster Prevention Day in Japan. On this day, schools, companies and towns hold earthquake drills. Japanese children learn to protect their heads, hide under their desks, and follow evacuation plans. Many families keep an emergency bag at home with water, food, a torch and a radio. Being prepared saves lives!

title: The road to war
text:
