In 1926, Emperor Hirohito came to the throne. His era was called [Shōwa], "enlightened peace". Sadly, the first part of his reign would be a time of terrible war.

In 1929, a worldwide economic crisis hit Japan hard. Farmers became very poor. Many people lost trust in politicians. Military officers, some of them very nationalist, became more and more powerful. They believed Japan should expand its empire to get land and resources.

In 1931, Japanese army officers in Manchuria, in northeast China, secretly blew up a railway and blamed Chinese soldiers. They used this as an excuse to take over all of Manchuria, without the government's permission. When the League of Nations, an organization of countries meant to keep peace, criticized Japan, Japan left it.

In 1937, a full war began between Japan and China, the Second Sino-Japanese War. The Japanese army committed terrible crimes against Chinese people, especially in the city of Nanjing, where a very large number of civilians and prisoners were killed. Millions of Chinese people died during this war.

In Japan, freedom disappeared. People who criticized the war could be arrested. Children were taught at school that dying for the emperor was the greatest honour.

In 1940, Japan allied with Nazi Germany and Fascist Italy. The United States stopped selling oil to Japan. On the 7th of December 1941, Japan launched a surprise attack on the American naval base of Pearl Harbor, in Hawaii. This started the Pacific War, part of World War II.

At first, Japan conquered a huge area: the Philippines, Indonesia, Malaysia, Burma and many Pacific islands. In these countries, many people suffered from forced labour and violence. But from 1942, the United States began winning battles. Many soldiers on both sides died on islands like Guadalcanal, Iwo Jima and Okinawa. In the Battle of Okinawa in 1945, about a quarter of the island's civilians died.

From 1944, American planes bombed Japanese cities. On the night of the 10th of March 1945, a firebombing raid on Tokyo killed about 100,000 people in one night. Children from the cities were evacuated to the countryside. Food was so scarce that people ate sweet potato leaves.

The war brought immense suffering to millions of people across Asia and to the Japanese people themselves.

title: Hiroshima, Nagasaki and the end of the war
text:
On the morning of the 6th of August 1945, at 8:15, an American plane called the Enola Gay dropped a new kind of bomb on the city of [Hiroshima]: an [atomic bomb].

In an instant, a blinding flash and a gigantic fireball destroyed the centre of the city. The heat was so intense that it left the shadows of people on stone steps. By the end of 1945, about 140,000 people had died. Three days later, on the 9th of August, a second atomic bomb was dropped on [Nagasaki], killing about 74,000 people by the end of the year.

Many survivors, called [hibakusha], suffered for the rest of their lives from burns and illnesses caused by [radiation], like cancer.

On the 15th of August 1945, Japanese people heard the voice of Emperor Hirohito on the radio for the very first time. Speaking in a formal, old-fashioned language, he announced that Japan accepted surrender. World War II was over.

One of the most moving stories is that of Sadako Sasaki. She was 2 years old when the bomb fell on Hiroshima, and she seemed to be fine. But at 12, she became very sick with leukaemia, caused by the radiation. In hospital, she began folding paper cranes, because a Japanese legend says that if you fold 1,000 cranes, your wish will come true. She folded more than 1,000, but sadly, she died in 1955.

Her classmates collected money to build a monument for her and all the children who died because of the bomb. On top of the Children's Peace Monument in Hiroshima stands a statue of Sadako holding a golden crane. Every year, children from all over the world send millions of paper cranes to it. The words at its base say: "This is our cry. This is our prayer. Peace in the world."

The ruins of one building near the centre of the explosion were left as they were: the Atomic Bomb Dome. It is now a UNESCO World Heritage site, a reminder of the horrors of nuclear weapons.

Every year on the 6th and 9th of August, ceremonies are held in Hiroshima and Nagasaki, and at 8:15 and 11:02, all of Japan observes a minute of silence to pray for peace. In 2024, Nihon Hidankyō, an organization of atomic bomb survivors, received the Nobel Peace Prize for its work for a world without nuclear weapons.

title: A new constitution for peace
text:
After the war, Japan was in ruins. Cities had been burned, millions of people had lost their homes, and there was very little food. Many children had lost their parents.

From 1945 to 1952, Japan was [occupied] by the Allied forces, mainly the Americans, led by General Douglas MacArthur. It was the first time in its history that Japan had been occupied by a foreign army.

The occupation authorities wanted to make sure Japan would never go to war again and would become a [democracy]. Many big changes were made:
- The army and navy were dissolved.
- Big landowners had to sell their land cheaply to the farmers who worked it.
- Workers were allowed to form trade unions.
- Schools were reformed, and textbooks that glorified war were changed. At first, students even had to black out passages in their old textbooks with ink!
- Women got the right to vote! In the 1946 elections, 39 women were elected to parliament.

In 1946, Emperor Hirohito declared that he was not a god, but a human being.

On the 3rd of May 1947, the new Constitution of Japan came into force. It is still Japan's constitution today, and it has never been changed! It says that:
- power belongs to the people,
- the emperor is "the symbol of the State and of the unity of the people", with no political power,
- everyone has fundamental rights: freedom of speech, of religion, equality between men and women...
- and in its famous [Article 9], Japan renounces war forever as a way to solve conflicts between nations.

Because of Article 9, Japan has no official army. Instead, it created the [Self-Defense Forces] in 1954, which are only supposed to defend Japan. They are also often seen helping people after earthquakes and other disasters. Some Japanese people want to change Article 9, while many others want to keep it as a symbol of peace. It's a big debate in Japan.

The 3rd of May is now a national holiday: Constitution Memorial Day. It's part of "Golden Week", a series of holidays in spring when many Japanese families go on trips.

In 1951, Japan signed a peace treaty in San Francisco, and in 1952 it became independent again. In 1956, it joined the [United Nations].

title: Astro Boy and Godzilla: manga and monsters
text:
In the difficult years after the war, Japanese children and adults needed dreams and fun. They found them in manga and cinema!

[Manga] are Japanese comics. Their roots go back to funny animal drawings from the 12th century and Hokusai's sketchbooks. But modern manga really took off after the war, thanks to one man: Osamu Tezuka.

Tezuka was born in 1928. As a child, he loved insects, Disney cartoons and drawing. During the war, he survived bombing raids in Osaka. After the war, he studied to become a doctor... but he couldn't stop drawing!

In 1952, he began a manga called "Astro Boy" (Tetsuwan Atom in Japanese). It's the story of a little robot boy with a kind heart and superpowers, who has rocket boots and fights for peace between humans and robots. Children loved it! In 1963, it became one of the first Japanese animated TV series, the ancestor of today's [anime].

Tezuka used techniques from cinema: close-ups, different angles, movement lines, and big expressive eyes inspired by Disney. He drew more than 150,000 pages in his life, with stories for children, for adults, about medicine, history, and even the life of the Buddha! He is called "the God of Manga". Many great manga artists were inspired by him.

In 1954, a giant monster appeared on Japanese cinema screens: Godzilla (Gojira in Japanese, a mix of "gorilla" and "kujira", whale). In the film, Godzilla is a prehistoric creature woken up by nuclear bomb tests, who attacks Tokyo with his radioactive breath.

Why was Godzilla so powerful for Japanese audiences? Because the film was about their real fears: the atomic bombs of Hiroshima and Nagasaki, and a real incident that same year, when a Japanese fishing boat, the Lucky Dragon No. 5, was exposed to radiation from an American nuclear test. Godzilla was a symbol of the dangers of nuclear weapons.

To make the monster, an actor wore a heavy rubber suit and walked through miniature models of Tokyo! Godzilla became a worldwide star, with more than 35 films. In 2024, a Japanese Godzilla film even won an Oscar for its visual effects!

Today, manga and anime are read and watched all over the world, and they are one of the most famous parts of Japanese culture.

title: The Shinkansen and the Tokyo Olympics
text:
In the 1950s and 1960s, Japan's economy grew incredibly fast. Factories made steel, ships, cameras, radios, televisions and cars. People worked very hard, and life got better year after year. This period is called the Japanese economic miracle.

In 1964, Japan wanted to show the world that it had recovered from the war and become a modern, peaceful country. Two great events did just that.

On the 1st of October 1964, the Shinkansen began running between Tokyo and Osaka. It was the first high-speed train in the world! It reached 210 km/h, and cut the journey time from about 6 hours and 40 minutes to 4 hours. Its rounded nose, a bit like an airplane, made it look like a bullet, so foreigners called it the "[bullet train]".

The Shinkansen runs on the route of the old Tōkaidō road, where samurai processions used to walk! Today, Shinkansen lines cover most of Japan, and trains reach up to 320 km/h. They are famous for being extremely punctual: the average delay is less than one minute! And in 60 years, no passenger has ever died in a Shinkansen accident. When a train arrives at its terminus, cleaning teams clean the whole train in just 7 minutes, then bow to the passengers!

Ten days later, on the 10th of October 1964, the Tokyo Olympic Games opened. They were the first Olympic Games ever held in Asia. The final torchbearer who lit the Olympic flame was Yoshinori Sakai, a 19-year-old student born in Hiroshima on the 6th of August 1945, the day of the atomic bomb. He was chosen as a symbol of Japan's rebirth and of peace.

The Games were broadcast by satellite to other countries for the first time. Judo appeared for the first time as an Olympic sport. The Japanese women's volleyball team, nicknamed "the Witches of the Orient", won the gold medal, and almost everyone in Japan watched the final on TV!

To get ready, Tokyo built new highways, a monorail to the airport, hotels and stadiums. Many families bought their first colour television to watch the Games.

In the 1960s, Japanese families dreamed of the "three Cs": a car, a colour TV and a cooler (air conditioner).

title: Expo '70: Osaka welcomes the world
text:
In 1968, Japan's economy became the second largest in the world, after the United States. Japanese brands like Sony, Toyota, Honda, Panasonic and Canon were becoming known everywhere.

In 1970, Japan held the first [World's Fair] in Asia: Expo '70 in Osaka. Its theme was "Progress and Harmony for Mankind". For six months, 77 countries showed off their technology and culture in amazing pavilions. More than 64 million visitors came! That was a record that lasted 40 years.

Visitors saw wonders of the future: moving walkways, video phones, early mobile phones, a robot band, and the first "human washing machine", a capsule that washed you automatically! The American pavilion displayed a real Moon rock brought back by the Apollo 12 astronauts. People waited up to four hours in line to see it!

The symbol of Expo '70 was the strange and powerful Tower of the Sun, created by the artist Tarō Okamoto. It's 70 metres high, with three faces: a golden face at the top representing the future, a face on the front representing the present, and a black face on the back representing the past. It still stands in Expo Park in Osaka today, and you can even visit the inside!

A lot of "everyday Japanese" things we know today appeared in this period. In 1958, Momofuku Andō invented instant ramen, and in 1971 he launched Cup Noodle! Convenience stores, or "konbini", and family restaurants began to spread in the 1970s.

But this rapid growth also had a dark side. Factories polluted the air, rivers and seas. The worst case was in the town of Minamata, in Kyushu. A chemical factory released mercury into the sea for years. People who ate the fish became very sick: they had trouble walking, speaking and seeing, and many died. Children were born with disabilities. This was called Minamata disease. The victims and their families fought for years to be recognized and helped.

These pollution disasters led Japan to create strict laws to protect the environment in the 1970s. The skies and rivers became cleaner. Today, Japan is known for its clean cities, and the lesson of Minamata is taught around the world.

title: The Famicom and the age of video games
text:
Do you like video games? Then you owe a lot to Japan!

Nintendo is a very old company. It was founded in Kyoto in 1889, and it started by making [hanafuda], traditional Japanese playing cards with pictures of flowers! Over the years, it tried many businesses, including a taxi company and instant rice, before making toys and then video games.

In 1981, a young designer named Shigeru Miyamoto created the arcade game "Donkey Kong", starring a little carpenter who had to save a girl from a big gorilla. That little man later became... Mario!

On the 15th of July 1983, Nintendo released a video game console for the home: the Family Computer, or "Famicom". It was red and white. Outside Japan, it was released as the "NES". It was a huge success, selling more than 60 million units around the world.

In 1985, "Super Mario Bros." came out. Mario runs, jumps on mushrooms, goes down pipes and rescues Princess Peach from Bowser. Miyamoto said he got ideas from his childhood, exploring the forests, caves and lakes around Kyoto. It became one of the best-selling games of all time. In 1986, Miyamoto also created "The Legend of Zelda", an adventure game inspired by his explorations as a child.

Japan became the world capital of video games. Sega created Sonic the Hedgehog, a fast blue hedgehog, to compete with Mario. Sony launched the PlayStation in 1994.

In 1996, a game appeared that became a worldwide phenomenon: Pokémon! Its creator, Satoshi Tajiri, loved collecting insects as a child in the countryside near Tokyo. He wanted children in the city to enjoy the fun of finding, collecting and exchanging creatures. Pokémon games, cartoons, cards and toys became a global craze. Pikachu is now one of the most famous characters in the world!

Japanese game makers also invented many kinds of games we play today, like Tetris-like puzzles on the Game Boy (1989), racing games, fighting games and role-playing games.

In 2017, Nintendo released the Switch, a console you can play on the TV or carry around. In 2025, it released the Switch 2. Video games are now one of Japan's most important cultural exports, along with manga and anime.

title: The start of Heisei and the bubble economy
text:
On the 7th of January 1989, Emperor Hirohito died after reigning for 62 years, the longest reign of any Japanese emperor. His son, Akihito, became emperor, and a new era began: Heisei, meaning "achieving peace".

Do you know how Japanese eras work? Japan still uses [era names] alongside the Western calendar. Each new emperor starts a new era. For example, 2025 is also "Reiwa 7". Many official documents in Japan use these era years!

At the end of the 1980s, Japan was incredibly rich. This time is called the [bubble economy]. Prices of land and shares rose to crazy levels. People said that the land around the Imperial Palace in Tokyo was worth more than all the land in California! Companies bought famous buildings in New York and famous paintings like Van Gogh's "Sunflowers". People spent money on luxury goods, and taxis were hard to find at night because everyone went out partying.

But a bubble always bursts. In 1990 and 1991, prices of shares and land crashed. Banks had lent huge amounts of money that could not be paid back. Companies went bankrupt. For more than 20 years, Japan's economy grew very slowly. This period is sometimes called the "Lost Decades". Many young people found it hard to get a stable job.

In 1995, two terrible events shocked Japan. On the 17th of January, a powerful earthquake struck the city of Kobe, killing more than 6,400 people. It's called the Great Hanshin earthquake. Thousands of volunteers from all over Japan came to help, so 1995 is sometimes called "year one of volunteering" in Japan. Then, in March, members of a cult released a poison gas called sarin in the Tokyo subway, killing 14 people and injuring many others.

Despite these difficulties, the Heisei era was also a time of peace. Emperor Akihito and Empress Michiko travelled across Japan and abroad, visiting disaster victims, kneeling to speak to them at eye level, and praying at former battlefields for the victims of the war.

During Heisei, Japan also became an [ageing society]: people live longer than almost anywhere in the world, but fewer babies are born. By 2025, almost 30% of Japanese people were over 65!

title: Studio Ghibli and Spirited Away
text:
Have you ever seen "My Neighbour Totoro", "Kiki's Delivery Service" or "Ponyo"? These films were made by a famous Japanese animation studio: Studio Ghibli.

Studio Ghibli was founded in 1985 by the directors Hayao Miyazaki and Isao Takahata, with the producer Toshio Suzuki. The name "Ghibli" comes from an Italian name for a hot desert wind. They wanted to blow a new wind into the world of animation!

Miyazaki was born in Tokyo in 1941. His father's company made parts for airplanes, which is why his films are often full of amazing flying machines. As a child, he loved reading manga and drawing.

Ghibli films are special. Most of them are drawn by hand, with thousands of beautiful, detailed drawings. They often have brave young heroines, like Nausicaä, Kiki, Chihiro and San. They talk about the beauty of nature, respect for the environment, the horrors of war, and kindness, with magical creatures and delicious-looking food!

In 1988, "My Neighbour Totoro" came out. It tells the story of two sisters who move to the countryside and meet Totoro, a huge, fluffy forest spirit who rides a Catbus! Totoro became the logo of the studio.

In 2001, Miyazaki released "Spirited Away" (Sen to Chihiro no Kamikakushi). It tells the story of Chihiro, a 10-year-old girl who enters a magical world of spirits. Her parents are turned into pigs, and she has to work in a bathhouse for gods to save them. It became the most successful film in the history of Japanese cinema! In 2003, it won the [Academy Award] (Oscar) for best animated feature film. It was the first non-English-language film to win it.

Isao Takahata, Miyazaki's friend and partner, made "Grave of the Fireflies" (1988), a very moving film about two children trying to survive at the end of the war, and "The Tale of the Princess Kaguya", based on a 10th-century Japanese folk tale.

In 2001, the Ghibli Museum opened in Mitaka, Tokyo. On its roof stands a giant robot from "Castle in the Sky". In 2022, a Ghibli Park opened in Aichi.

In 2024, Miyazaki won a second Oscar for "The Boy and the Heron". Ghibli films are loved all over the world!

title: The Great East Japan Earthquake
text:
On the 11th of March 2011, at 2:46 in the afternoon, the ground began to shake in northeastern Japan. It was one of the most powerful earthquakes ever recorded in the world: magnitude 9.0! In Tokyo, 300 kilometres away, skyscrapers swayed for minutes.

About 30 to 60 minutes later, something even more terrible arrived: a gigantic [tsunami]. In some places, the waves were more than 15 metres high, and water rushed up to 40 metres above sea level! The tsunami swept away entire towns along the coast of the Tōhoku region: houses, cars, boats, schools.

About 18,000 people died or disappeared. More than 400,000 people had to leave their homes.

The tsunami also hit the Fukushima Daiichi nuclear power plant. The electricity and cooling systems stopped, and three reactors melted down. Radioactive material was released into the air and sea. More than 100,000 people living nearby had to be evacuated, and some areas are still closed today. It was the worst nuclear accident since Chernobyl in 1986. After the accident, Japan stopped all its nuclear power plants for a while and began a big debate about energy.

In the middle of this tragedy, there were also stories of courage and solidarity. In the town of Kamaishi, almost all the schoolchildren survived because they had practised evacuation drills and ran to high ground on their own, even helping younger children and old people. This was called the "Kamaishi miracle". Around the world, people sent help and messages of support. Despite the chaos, there was no looting, and people waited patiently in line for water and food, which impressed the world.

In the town of Rikuzentakata, out of 70,000 pine trees along the beach, only one survived the tsunami. It became a symbol of hope, called the "Miracle Pine". When it died because of the salt water, it was preserved and restored as a monument.

After the disaster, many old stone markers were rediscovered along the coast. Some had been placed by people after tsunamis long ago, with warnings like: "Do not build your homes below this point." Today, new sea walls have been built, and every year on the 11th of March, Japan remembers the victims with a minute of silence at 2:46.

title: Reiwa and the Tokyo Olympics without spectators
text:
In 2016, Emperor Akihito, then 82 years old, spoke to the nation on television. He said he was worried that his age would soon make it hard for him to carry out his duties. This was very unusual! No Japanese emperor had stepped down in more than 200 years. A special law was passed to allow it.

On the 30th of April 2019, Akihito [abdicated]. The next day, the 1st of May, his son Naruhito became the 126th emperor of Japan, and a new era began: Reiwa.

"Reiwa" was chosen from a poem in the Man'yōshū, the oldest collection of Japanese poetry, from the 8th century. The poem describes plum blossoms opening in early spring in a gentle breeze. It was the first time an era name came from a Japanese book rather than a Chinese classic! "Reiwa" is often translated as "beautiful harmony".

When the name was announced on television, a government official held up a board with the two characters written in beautiful calligraphy. People all over Japan celebrated the new era with countdown parties, as if it were New Year!

Emperor Naruhito studied at Oxford University in England, and he is an expert on the history of water transport on rivers. Empress Masako was a diplomat before her marriage and speaks several languages.

Tokyo had been chosen to host the Olympic Games in 2020. But in early 2020, the world was hit by the [COVID-19 pandemic]. For the first time in history, the Olympic Games were postponed by one year.

The Tokyo Olympics finally took place in the summer of 2021, but almost without spectators, to prevent the virus from spreading. Athletes competed in empty stadiums, with recorded cheers and the support of millions of people watching on TV. New sports appeared, like skateboarding, surfing, sport climbing and karate. Japan won 27 gold medals, its best result ever! Young Japanese skateboarders, some only 13 years old, won medals and became stars.

The medals of these Games were made from recycled metals collected from about 79,000 tonnes of old phones and electronic devices donated by people across Japan!

The Reiwa era has also seen many visitors come to Japan from around the world, attracted by its food, culture, nature and anime. In 2024, Japan welcomed more than 36 million foreign tourists, a record.

title: Japan today: tradition and the future
text:
Here we are in today's Japan! What is it like?

Japan has about 124 million inhabitants. Its capital, Tokyo, together with its surrounding area, is the largest city in the world, with about 37 million people! Japan is a peaceful democracy, with a parliament, a prime minister, and an emperor who is a symbol of the nation. In 2025, Japan had its first woman prime minister, Sanae Takaichi.

In 2025, Japan hosted a World Expo again, in Osaka, on an artificial island called Yumeshima, "Dream Island". The theme was "Designing Future Society for Our Lives". Its symbol was the "Grand Ring", a giant circle of wooden walkways, 2 kilometres around. It entered the Guinness World Records as the largest wooden structure in the world! Its funny mascot, Myaku-Myaku, with red cells and blue body, became very popular.

Japan is known for its advanced technology: robots, high-speed trains, electronics, and space exploration. In 2024, a Japanese spacecraft called SLIM landed precisely on the Moon! Japanese space probes have even brought back samples from asteroids.

But Japan also keeps its old traditions alive. People visit shrines at New Year, admire cherry blossoms in spring during [hanami], wear yukata at summer festivals, and see fireworks. Children celebrate Children's Day on the 5th of May with carp-shaped streamers, and the Shichi-Go-San festival at 3, 5 and 7 years old.

Japanese food, [washoku], is listed by UNESCO as an Intangible Cultural Heritage. Sushi, ramen, tempura, onigiri and bento boxes are loved all over the world!

Japan faces big challenges too: its population is ageing and shrinking, and fewer babies are born. It must also prepare for earthquakes, typhoons and the effects of climate change. More and more people from other countries come to live and work in Japan, making it more diverse.

Japanese culture has spread all over the planet: manga, anime, video games, karaoke, emoji (a Japanese word meaning "picture character"!), and ideas like [kaizen] (continuous improvement), and "mottainai", the feeling that it's a pity to waste anything.

The story of Japan is still being written, from the first hunters of the Ice Age to the children of today. What would you like to add?
